To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the lambda-dimension of a graph in SCET is given by: lambda = 1 + 3N_s + 2N_g + 2N_c, where N_s, N_g, and N_c are respectively the number of soft, collinear, and hard vertices.

the lambda-dimension of an SCET operator can be determined solely from its vertices, that it is gauge invariant, that it can be applied to processes that do not have a conventional OPE, that it has a correspondence with the dynamical twist of an operator in a conventional OPE and that it has a simple correspondence with the number of soft-collinear loops.
we have derived a power counting rule that can be used to determine whether a given operator in SCET has the right scaling behavior for the infrared physics of a process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) What is the correct power counting for SCET? (2) How does the SCET power counting relate to the traditional OPE? (3) What is the relation of SCET to the OPE?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SCET provides a framework to systematically analyze the infrared region of QCD processes in a way that is independent of the process, gauge invariant and that can be extended to all orders in lambda.
the lambda-expansion is an expansion in the number of soft and collinear degrees of freedom.
the SCET power counting rule is an effective field theory version of the usual twist counting rule.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have derived a power counting formula in SCET which has a correspondence with a dynamical twist formula.
we have developed a systematic procedure for determining the operators that are necessary to describe the infrared at a given order in the lambda expansion.
we have found a simple way to assign the lambda-dimension of a process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lambda-dimension of a graph in SCET is the sum of the lambda-dimensions of the vertices.
the lambda-dimension of a graph is equal to the number of soft vertices plus the number of collinear vertices, plus the number of soft-collinear vertices minus the number of external lines.
the lambda-dimension of an SCET graph can be determined solely from the vertices.
